questions.stem: Which of the following is the best definition of span of control?
options: The number of employees who report directly to one manager
The number of levels of authority in a business
The line of authority from the top of a business to the bottom
The number of decisions a manager makes each day
questions.why: Span of control is horizontal: how many people one manager supervises. Wide spans force delegation; narrow spans allow close supervision.
whyNot: That is the hierarchy, or the number of layers.
That is the chain of command, which is vertical.
Not a recognised measure of structure.

questions.stem: Which term is defined as: the line of authority through which instructions pass from the top of a business to the bottom?
options: Chain of command
Span of control
Matrix structure
Delayering
questions.why: The chain of command is vertical. More layers means a longer chain, which slows communication and distorts it.
whyNot: Span of control is how many report to one manager, which is horizontal.
A matrix structure groups employees into cross-functional project teams.
Delayering removes levels of hierarchy.

questions.stem: A tall organisational structure is characterised by:
options: many levels of hierarchy and narrow spans of control
few levels of hierarchy and wide spans of control
many levels of hierarchy and wide spans of control
no hierarchy at all
questions.why: For a given number of employees, narrow spans require more layers to cover everyone, which is what makes the structure tall.
whyNot: That describes a flat structure.
These cannot both apply in an organisation of fixed size: wide spans mean fewer layers are needed.
Every organisation of any size has some hierarchy.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the best definition of decentralisation?
options: Delegating decision-making authority to lower levels of the organisation
Keeping all decision-making authority at the top
Removing levels of hierarchy
Moving offices to different locations
questions.why: Decentralisation pushes authority down, which speeds up local decisions, uses local knowledge and motivates staff by giving them responsibility.
whyNot: That is centralisation.
That is delayering, which changes the shape rather than where decisions are taken.
That is geographic dispersion, which is not the same as decentralised authority.

questions.stem: What is the main effect of a long chain of command on communication?
options: It becomes slower and more likely to be distorted
It becomes faster and clearer
It has no effect on communication
It removes the need for written instructions
questions.why: Every layer a message passes through adds delay and a chance of being changed or misunderstood, which is one of the main arguments for delayering.
whyNot: Fewer layers, not more, make communication faster and more direct.
The number of layers a message passes through is one of the main influences on it.
More layers usually means more formal documentation, not less.

questions.stem: What is the main drawback of a matrix structure?
options: Employees report to two managers, which creates conflicting priorities
It prevents specialists from working together
It has no hierarchy at all
It is only possible in businesses with one product
questions.why: The two-bosses problem is the central weakness: a project leader and a functional manager can both want the same person's time, and it is unclear who decides.
whyNot: Bringing specialists together across functions is exactly what a matrix is for.
There is still a functional hierarchy; the project structure sits across it.
Matrix structures are typically used by businesses running multiple projects or products.

questions.stem: Why can decentralisation be motivating for employees?
options: It gives them responsibility, which Herzberg identifies as a genuine motivator
It reduces the amount of work they have to do
It guarantees a pay rise
It removes all supervision
questions.why: Responsibility and involvement are on Herzberg's motivator list. That is why structure connects directly to the motivation topic rather than being purely administrative.
whyNot: It usually means more responsibility and often more work.
Authority and pay are separate decisions.
Decentralisation delegates authority; it does not remove accountability or oversight.

questions.stem: A business delayers, removing a level of middle management. What is the likely trade-off?
options: Lower wage costs and faster decisions, but lost experience and stretched managers
Higher wage costs and slower decisions
No change to communication or cost
A longer chain of command
questions.why: Delayering saves the salaries and speeds up the chain, and it also removes people who held informal knowledge and mentored others, while widening the spans of those who remain.
whyNot: Removing managers lowers the wage bill and shortens the chain.
Both cost and communication are directly affected.
Removing a layer shortens the chain of command.

questions.stem: Why is it too simple to say a business should be either centralised or decentralised?
options: Most businesses centralise some decisions and decentralise others
Centralisation is illegal in most countries
Decentralisation only applies to manufacturing
The two terms mean the same thing
questions.why: A hotel group will centralise brand standards, pricing systems and procurement while decentralising how staff handle a guest complaint. Recognising that is the most sophisticated point available on this topic and very few candidates make it.
whyNot: Neither approach is a legal matter.
Both apply across every sector.
They are opposites: authority at the top against authority delegated down.

questions.stem: In which situation is a tall structure with narrow spans of control most justified?
options: Safety-critical work where close supervision genuinely matters
A small creative agency of six people
A business that wants the fastest possible decisions
A business trying to cut its management wage bill
questions.why: Where a mistake is dangerous, the cost of close supervision is worth paying. Narrow spans mean a manager can actually watch and check the work.
whyNot: Six people need almost no hierarchy; a tall structure would be absurd.
Tall structures slow decisions down because of the long chain.
Tall structures need more managers, so they raise the wage bill.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the best definition of a flat structure?
options: Few levels of hierarchy and wide spans of control
Many levels of hierarchy and narrow spans of control
A structure with no managers
A structure where everyone earns the same
questions.why: Few layers means each manager supervises more people, so delegation becomes necessary and decisions move faster.
whyNot: That is a tall structure.
Flat structures still have managers; there are simply fewer layers of them.
Pay equality is unrelated to the shape of the structure.

questions.stem: A flat structure can demotivate ambitious employees. Why?
options: There are few levels, so there are few promotions available
Flat structures pay less by law
Employees in flat structures have no responsibility
Flat structures have longer chains of command
questions.why: With few rungs on the ladder, the only way up is often out, so capable and ambitious people leave. That is the counterweight to the motivation benefits of flatter structures.
whyNot: Pay is not determined by structure.
Flat structures usually give MORE responsibility, through necessary delegation.
Flat structures have shorter chains, which is one of their advantages.
